30. We find that section 439(4) is a special provision and section 561A is a general provision of the Code, where there is in the same statute a specific provision and also a general one, which, in its most comprehensive sense, would include matters embraced in the former, the particular provision must be operative and the general provision must be taken to affect only such cases within its general language as are not within the provisions of the particular (special) provision. Reference in this connection may be made to the case of Mulgi Tri Bhuvan Sevak Vs. Dakor Municipality, AIR 1922 (Born) 247 (FB); Harman Singh Vs. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1967 (Bom) 482, 491; State Vs. Golam Singh, AIR 1965 (All) 300 Where a general expression is expressed and the Act expresses also a particular intention incompatible with the general intention, the particular intention is to be considered in the nature of an exception (Reference in this connection may be made to the case of Venkatesen Vs. Nikhil Chandra, AIR 1962 Calcutta 2581262). When there are two sections in a statute, one dealing specifically with any particular subject which is also included in some of the provisions of another section which is couched in general terms, the provisions of the former section must preval, unless there is a specific provision to the contrary in the (same) statute itself. (Valdeo Singh Vs. State, AIR 1951 Madha Bharat 149), Vithaeji Madharji Vs. IT Commissioner, AIR 1948 (Mad), 353, Bhana Mekan Vs. Emperor, AIR 1936 (Bom) 256; Union Insurance Society Vs. Md. Karam Elahi Khan, AIR 1934 Peswar 37; Ramnath Vs. King Emperor, AIR 1925 (All) 230. In other words, where the same statute makes general provisions in respect of a particular subject matter and makes specific provisions with respect to a special category, the latter must prevail over the general. Reference in this connection may be made to the case of Kameshwar Singh Vs. Province of Bihar, AIR 1950 Patna 391, 418; Jhotrirdra Naryan Vs. Purna Chandra, AIR 1950 Assam 161; Koraram Vs. Saling, AIR 1928 (All) 536 (Special provision should ordinarily receive effect unqualified by the general); Krishnamachari Vs. Shawallau and C, ILR 39 Madras 576; Vaidyanathlyer Vs. LIC Madras, AIR 1964 Madras 24, Nityanand Vs. Erramma, AIR 1962 Andhra Pradesh 394; Koshalya Rani Vs. Copal Singh, AIR 1963 (Pun) 145/148. Where there are specific provisions in a statute, whether it is substantiative or procedural law, the matter must be governed by special provision in preference to the general provision. When a provision deals with a special case it is not permissible to contend that the special case would also fall within the general provision in the (same) statute. Subodh Chandra Vs. IT and EPT Commissioner, AIR 1954 (Bom) 234 A special provision would prevail over the general provision unless, on a consideration of the statute in its entirety, a contrary, intention of the legislature is indicated as contained in the maxim generalia speciaibus non derogant (Anand Reddy Vs. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1959 Andhra 144, 146). Where there is general provision which, if applied in its entirety would neutralize a special provision dealing with the same subject matter, the special provision must be read as provision to the general provision and the general provision, in so far as it is inconsistent with the special provision, must be deemed not to apply (1908 Goodwesi Vs. Philips 7 CLR 14), Taylor Vs. Oldham Corporation 4 on. D. 395, 410; where there are two provisions which may possibly govern a case, the one more general and the other more particular and specific, the latter provision ought to be adopted. 

 45. The jurisdiction of the High Court Division has been absolutely barred by the legislature expressly under section 439(4) against an order passed by the Sessions Judge under section 439A. Where a jurisdiction of a superior Court (High Court Division) having been expressly taken away by a special provision of a statute, in respect of a subject, in our opinion, in such a case the superior Court (High Court Division) cannot under the same statute (could) take resort to a general provision to exercise its inherent power under section 561A to adjudicate upon the same subject. The jurisdiction of the High Court Division to revise or review an order passed by the Sessions Judge under section 439 had been absolutely taken away expressly by section 439(4) and as such it would amount to misinterpretation of a statute to interfere with the order of the Sessions Judge passed under section 439A. In other words, it would amount to legislate which is the jurisdiction of the legislature and not of the Court. In this connection reference may be made to the case of Sadananda Pyne Vs Harinam Shaho, reported in AIR 1950 (Cal) 179, wherein it was observed that "Courts must resist the temptation to change the law under cover of interpretation of law. If they abuse their power to interpret law, to alter laws which they' may not like, and to make new laws which they think should be made, that would be a corrupt use of their power". The function of the Court is to interpret the law and not to amend, modify and alter it (Ram Narayan Vs. Dinapur Cana Board, AIR 1958 Patna 71,72).
